countries.name: Finland
countries.headline: Finns read a national record in OmaKanta and decide by permit who outside their region sees it, but public bodies cannot yet be fined.

access.summary: OmaKanta shows visit notes, lab and imaging results, vaccinations and prescriptions from public and private care, and 3.3 million people used it in 2025. Records start only when a provider joined Kanta (from 2013), and no app can yet download them.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.headline: Danes see hospital records, labs and medicines on sundhed.dk and can block lookups, but GP notes are only now arriving and registers have no opt-out.

access.summary: The Commission gave Denmark a 98% eHealth maturity score for 2025, and over 3 million Danes use sundhed.dk or MinSundhed each year. GP notes are only starting to appear, and the full hospital record still needs an access request.

countries.name: Estonia
countries.headline: Every provider must feed one national record that patients can read, log-check and close, but police and security services can query it without consent.

access.summary: The Medical Records Act gives a right to a copy of the whole record, clarified by a 2025 amendment. Heilsuvera shows prescriptions, vaccinations and dates of hospital and clinic visits, but not clinical notes or lab results.

control.summary: Patients can ban sharing through linked record systems, for a whole provider, a department or a named party, and have a legal right to learn who looked at their record. Bans need a signed form, and the access log comes on request only.

journey.summary: A 2019 Nordic Council of Ministers report says all hospitals and primary care clinics share records over the national HealthNet, and every pharmacy is linked for e-prescriptions. Some private providers still keep non-digital records until a December 2026 deadline.

commercial.summary: The Medical Records Act bars any access to records without a legal basis, which shuts out insurers and employers by default. No Iceland-specific ban on selling health data or using it for marketing beyond GDPR was verified.

clinical.summary: Treating staff can reach records at other providers through linked systems unless the patient has banned it, and every doctor can see all prescriptions and dispensings. Patients can pre-authorise sharing of key data for emergency care elsewhere in the EEA.

Patients can bar identifiable storage in research health-data collections, but no general opt-out from record research was found.

countries.name: Israel
countries.headline: Every Israeli can read most of their record in their health fund's app, but the national exchange offers only an all-or-nothing opt-out.

access.summary: The Patient's Rights Act gives a right to the record and a copy, and a 2019 ministry circular makes all four health funds show members structured and free-text data online. No fixed deadline was found and no official usage figure was verified.

countries.name: Latvia
countries.headline: The E-veselība record, with an access log and patient bans, covers prescriptions, labs and discharges, but staff snooping persists and the portal is being rebuilt.

access.summary: The free national E-veselība portal shows prescriptions, referrals, discharge summaries and lab results (from 2024), and the law gives one free copy within three working days. Export and full history depth were not verified, so the score sits in the lower half of its band.

control.summary: Patients can see an audit log of who opened their record, ban all access or block chosen providers and data, and delegate access. Records are open to treating staff by default, and repeated snooping cases keep the score in the lower half of the band.

countries.name: Singapore
countries.headline: A 2026 law, not yet in force, makes every provider feed one national record without consent; patients can block access, but very few do.

access.summary: Patients can view medications, immunisations and lab results from the national record in HealthHub, and the PDPA gives a right to request the rest from each provider. But providers may charge a fee and need not hand over copies of doctors' notes.

control.summary: Data flows into the NEHR without consent, but a person can block all provider access and can see a one-year log of which institutions opened their record. Only about 2,300 people have placed a block since 2011, and finer choices in HealthHub are planned from 2027.

countries.name: Slovenia

countries.headline: Japanese patients see five years of claims-based records online and choose at each visit what doctors see, but full charts stay with each provider.

access.summary: The privacy law gives a right to a copy, electronic on request, and Mynaportal shows five years of claims-based treatment and medicine data. The law sets no fixed deadline and allows fees, so full charts still come provider by provider.

access.summary: Pakistan has no data protection law giving a right to a copy of one's record; the 2023 bill was withdrawn in a Senate committee. An older doctors' ethics code allows copies or summaries, with no deadline; the 2026 code's wording was not verified, and there is no portal.

control.summary: The only consent rule is in the doctors' ethics code: records must not be handed to anyone without the patient's consent. There is no opt-out, no access log and no digital consent tool, and providers decide in practice.

privacy.summary: Pakistan has no general or health data protection law, so health records rely on a criminal cyber law and professional confidentiality rules. Pakistan is not on the EU adequacy list, and the EU's EHDS does not apply.

countries.name: Papua New Guinea
countries.headline: Papua New Guinea has no data protection law in force, no patient portal, and electronic records in 4 of 3,234 health facilities.

access.summary: Section 51 of the Constitution gives citizens reasonable access to official documents, but no law sets a procedure, and the Right to Information Policy was only validated in June 2026. No health-specific right to a copy and no patient portal were verified.
